vignette:
Margaret is a 71-year-old forensic analyst who has spent decades examining physical evidence in a busy metropolitan crime lab. Five months ago, while working late, a man who had been brought in for questioning broke free from an interview room and cornered her in the hallway. He grabbed her by the neck, his fingers digging into her throat as he hissed that she would never see retirement-that there was no future for someone like her. She managed to hit the alarm, but the assault lasted only moments before security arrived. In that time, she had stared directly at his hands, at the specific way his knuckles whitened, and she had heard the exact words about her future being cut short.

After the attack, Margaret found herself trapped in a loop she could not name. The memory came in fragments: the pressure on her windpipe, the click of his ring against her collarbone. But when she tried to recall the full sequence, her mind would shove it away before she reached the end-she had come to believe that if she let herself finish remembering, she would shatter. Other times she could recall every detail with eerie clarity yet felt nothing, as if it had happened to a stranger. The blankness scared her almost as much as the rage that sometimes erupted without warning: a hot, blinding fury that left her shaking long after it passed.

She had always been a sharp, decisive woman, but now she felt fundamentally inadequate-she should have seen it coming, should have been stronger. That sense of failure hollowed out her old happiness; she told her husband she was just tired, but privately she knew she had become permanently miserable. And she was certain that dwelling on the event would destroy her, so she forced her thoughts elsewhere whenever the memory surfaced. That certainty-that she could not survive facing it-seemed to keep the memory raw and near, as if her fear of it was the very thing that made it so easy to find.

This vigilance reshaped her daily life. At work she avoided the hallway where it happened, and she refused to discuss the case with anyone, even her supervisor. Talking about the future-colleagues mentioning retirement parties, her husband planning a trip-sent a jolt through her chest, because she had been told she would not have one. That conviction also meant that she now saw threats everywhere-a man looking at her too long, a door left ajar, a raised voice-each one a potential sign that her future really was being cut short. Specific body parts became triggers too: a man's hands gripping a coffee cup, even the curve of a wrist, could flash her back to those whitened knuckles. Each reminder triggered a fresh wave of memory, and each memory reinforced her belief that she could not handle it.

Her maladaptive strategies grew into rigid routines. She now always sits with her back against a wall in any room, scanning the space for exits. But that very posture had turned every ordinary room into a fresh trigger: the solid wall at her back was a constant, silent reminder of why she needed it there, yanking her attention back to the attack each time she felt the plaster against her shoulder blades. She stopped exercising-the pounding of her own heart during a jog felt too close to the adrenaline of the attack. And the fact that she could no longer tolerate the feeling of her own heartbeat told her, with mounting certainty, that she had become someone too weak to handle ordinary life. And she began to undereat: food seemed heavy, and restricting it gave her a fleeting sense of control over a body that had failed her. These strategies, however, kept the trauma alive. Sitting against a wall reminded her why she did it; skipping meals left her tired, which made her more vulnerable to intrusive memories; and avoiding exercise meant she never released the tension that fed her hypervigilance.

The consequences accumulated. Her husband noticed she flinched when he touched her neck, and she had snapped at him once when he asked about retirement. Her performance at work slipped-she missed details in a report, and a colleague had to cover for her. She felt more inadequate than ever, and the misery deepened. What finally brought Margaret to seek help was a moment in the lab when a junior analyst, gesturing while explaining a new procedure, held up his hand in a way that made her see the assailant's fingers again. She fled to the bathroom, heart racing, and realized she could no longer function. Sitting in the intake office, she whispered that she just wanted to feel like herself again-but she was terrified that trying to heal would mean facing everything she had been avoiding.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not show that maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance, undereating, scanning) cause or lead to triggers. While strategies are described as responses to triggers, there is no causal link from strategies to the development or exacerbation of triggers.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not show that maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance, undereating, scanning) cause or lead to triggers. While strategies are described as responses to triggers, there is no causal link from strategies to the development or exacerbation of triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."

No paragraph shows that negative appraisals lead to the development of triggers; triggers are associated with the memory of the assault.
No paragraph shows that maladaptive strategies directly cause negative appraisals; the connection is indirect and not within the same paragraph.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals cause the intrusive memory; instead, memory reinforces appraisals.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph shows that negative appraisals lead to the development of triggers; triggers are associated with the memory of the assault.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph shows that maladaptive strategies directly cause negative appraisals; the connection is indirect and not within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
